query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Using additive friction stir deposition (AFSD) to process AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock will overcome the drawbacks of conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing by promoting solid‐state deposition that minimizes thermal gradients, reduces residual stresses, and preserves or even enhances mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock prepared via mechanical alloying to produce a homogeneous multi‐principal element material with a fine dispersion of phases.
generation.intervention: Replace high-thermal-load AM techniques (e.g., laser melting) with a solid-state, friction stir based deposition process (AFSD) tailored for miniature component fabrication.
generation.conditions: AFSD processing under controlled tool speeds and applied load, using a deposition setup optimized for miniature geometries (e.g., layered structures with dimensions suited to small components) at temperatures sufficiently high for plastic flow but below the melting point. Testing should be conducted under ambient to moderately elevated ambient conditions to maintain a solid-state process window.
generation.structural_mediator: The severe plastic deformation and frictional heating inherent to AFSD that refine the grain structure into uniform, equiaxed grains while limiting the formation of high-magnitude thermal gradients.
generation.mechanism: AFSD generates frictional heat and imposes intense plastic deformation without reaching full melting. This solid‐state process minimizes phase changes and sharp thermal gradients, thereby reducing the buildup of residual tensile stresses and preventing microstructural degradation that typically occur during rapid solidification in fusion-based AM.
generation.predicted_outcome: Miniature components fabricated via AFSD will exhibit significantly lower residual stress levels (potentially a reduction by over 50% relative to conventional methods) and improved mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength and ductility retained or enhanced) compared to components produced under conventional high-thermal-load regimes.
generation.baseline: Components produced by conventional additive manufacturing processes (e.g., laser powder bed fusion) which suffer from high thermal gradients, residual tensile stresses, and degraded microstructure due to rapid melting/solidification cycles.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for AlCrFeNiSi-based miniature components processed under optimized AFSD conditions. The applicability to larger-scale components or to alloys with substantially different thermal or mechanical behavior remains to be established.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements in mechanical properties and the extent of residual stress reduction are not fully predictable without process parameter optimization. Additionally, long-term stability and scaling effects require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of miniature components using AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock: one set using conventional high-thermal-load AM (e.g., laser melting) and the other using the AFSD process. Ensure that both sets share identical geometries and similar build parameters aside from the deposition method. After fabrication, perform residual stress measurements, microstructural characterization, and mechanical testing.
measurements: Residual stress mapping using X-ray diffraction and/or neutron diffraction
Microstructural analysis via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD)
Mechanical testing including tensile tests and hardness measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If components fabricated via AFSD do not show a statistically significant reduction in residual stresses (e.g., less than 50% lower than those from conventional AM) or if their mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility) are not at least maintained or improved relative to conventional builds, then the hypothesis will be refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Post-processing T6 heat treatment of AFSD-manufactured Al6061 has been shown to successfully restore the mechanical properties to those expected for the T6 condition []. For Al6063, the post-processing T6 heat treatment was reported to eliminate the hardness gradient similar to that noted in Figure 4a–c []. The solutionising step of the T6 heat treatment process exposes the material to a temperature greater than 500 °C [], which softens the material and allows for plastic flow and residual stress relief. Meanwhile, during the quenching and ageing steps, a different residual stress profile is expected to form, which is dependent on the structure geometry [].

Metal additive manufacturing (AM) is a low-cost, high-efficiency functional mold manufacturing technology. However, when the functional section of the mold or part is not a partial area, and large-area additive processing of high-hardness metal is required, cracks occur frequently in AM and substrate materials owing to thermal stress and the accumulation of residual stresses. Hence, research on residual stress reduction technologies is required. In this study, we investigated the effect of reducing residual stress due to thermal deviation reduction using a real-time heating device as well as changes in laser power in the AM process for both high-hardness cold and hot work mold steel. The residual stress was measured using an X-ray stress diffraction device before and after AM. Compared to the AM processing conditions at room temperature (25 °C), residual stress decreased by 57% when the thermal deviation was reduced. The microstructures and mechanical properties of AM specimens manufactured under room-temperature and real-time preheating and heating conditions were analyzed using an optical microscope.
